Bilva Consumer Care: Two Lakh Outlets and Nowhere to Look

The company had trebled its reach in thirty months. Nobody in the room could say, with a number they trusted, whether more people were using the product.

1. Alwarpet, Chennai — Sunday, 20 September 2026

The power had gone out on Eldams Road at a quarter past nine, and Aparna Venkataraman worked for forty minutes by the light of her laptop before the inverter in the building settled into its hum. On the dining table in front of her were three printouts, each of which claimed to describe the same financial year, and none of which agreed with the other two.

The first said that Bilva Consumer Care had shipped ₹212.4 crore of product in FY26, up from ₹167 crore, and that this was the best year in the company's ten-year history. The second said that its distributors had sold ₹180.7 crore onward to retailers. The third — a four-city retail panel Bilva had resumed subscribing to only in January, after a gap of twenty months — put consumer offtake at about ₹163 crore, and carried a footnote in six-point type that Aparna had read perhaps thirty times since Thursday.

On Tuesday morning, 22 September, the board would meet in Coimbatore to approve the FY27 annual operating plan and release the festive trade budget of ₹14 crore. Navratri began on 11 October; Diwali fell on 8 November; the co-packer in Hosur needed line bookings by 3 October, and the modern-trade chains would freeze their festive planograms in the second week of October. Whatever was decided on Tuesday would be irreversible by the end of the month.

Three proposals had been circulated, and each of the three was internally coherent. Harish Bhatia wanted the money spent on adding 1.15 lakh new general-trade outlets across Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal. Aparna's own category team wanted it spent on depth: a 45 ml pack, a visibility programme and a service-level fix in the 41,000 outlets that actually bought every month. Sneha Kulkarni wanted it spent on festive visibility across Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart, where Bilva's revenue had more than doubled in a year.

What kept Aparna at the table past eleven was not the choice between the three. It was a sentence Priya Ramesh had put in a message from Toronto on Friday evening and then, ninety seconds later, deleted — not quickly enough. We can measure how many shops we sell into. We cannot measure whether anyone is buying the second bottle. Aparna had screenshotted it before it vanished.

2. Bilva Consumer Care

Bilva was founded in Coimbatore in 2016 by Dr. Anil Menon, an Ayurvedic formulator who had spent eleven years in contract manufacturing for larger houses, and his cousin Meenakshi Rao, a chartered accountant who became the company's CFO and never left the role. The founding product, Bilva Amla-Bhringraj hair oil, was positioned between the mass coconut-oil brands and the premium herbal range: a 100 ml bottle at ₹96, later a 200 ml at ₹175, made on a cold-process line in Coimbatore and licensed as an Ayurvedic proprietary medicine under the state AYUSH authority rather than as a cosmetic. A second line, Bilva Ubtan face wash, launched in 2021 and contributed about a sixth of revenue. The hair oil was the company.

For its first six years Bilva grew the way small South Indian FMCG companies grow: distributor by distributor, out of Coimbatore into Tamil Nadu, then Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka, with a sales force that knew its retailers by name. By FY23 the company was at ₹84 crore with roughly 44,000 outlets and a reputation, among the chains, for a brand that sold slowly but sold steadily.

In March 2024 the board took the decision that shapes everything the company can do today. Kaveri Growth Partners had put ₹60 crore in at a valuation set explicitly on reach and dispatch revenue; the growth plan the money bought was called Project Kadam, and it committed Bilva to two lakh billed outlets within twenty-four months. Kadam needed funding inside the operating budget. Two things were cut to find it. The first was the company's syndicated retail-measurement subscription, which cost ₹1.35 crore a year and which Harish Bhatia argued — with some justice, at the time — told them mostly what they already knew about five states they already dominated. The second was a planned fifth regional depot.

The ₹1.35 crore went into Bilva Netra, a field-force and distributor-management application built by Yusuf Shaikh's team in Pune with a front-end pod in Bengaluru. Netra was genuinely good. It captured salesman beat plans, retailer orders, distributor stock and, optionally, shelf photographs. Within eighteen months it covered 71 per cent of distributors by value. What it could not do, because no field application can, was see a consumer. It measured what Bilva sold to the trade. For twenty months, until the panel was restored in January 2026 for four cities only, that was the only measurement the company had.

3. The Category

Indian hair oil is one of the most thoroughly contested shelves in the country. Marico's Parachute and Nihar, Dabur's Amla range, Bajaj Consumer Care's Almond Drops, Emami's Kesh King and Navratna, Hindustan Unilever's Indulekha, Himalaya, Patanjali and a dense regional tail together occupy a bay that a typical urban kirana gives perhaps three feet and eighteen facings. The large houses run direct distribution to a million-plus outlets; their salesmen visit weekly; their trade schemes reset monthly. A brand at Bilva's scale is, in every store, a guest.

Three structural forces had moved under the category in the two years of Project Kadam. The first was quick commerce. Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart had turned a category with low purchase urgency into one with high replenishment convenience, and had done it through a few thousand dark stores rather than a few lakh shops — a distribution structure with completely different arithmetic. The second was the rise of digital-first personal-care brands such as Mamaearth and WOW, which had demonstrated that a brand could build national consumer awareness with almost no physical distribution and then walk into modern trade holding the awareness as a bargaining chip. The third was regulatory: the Central Consumer Protection Authority and ASCI had both tightened their reading of hair-growth and Ayurvedic efficacy claims, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act had made Bilva's legal counsel unhappy about Netra's photograph feature, which routinely captured shopkeepers' faces and phone numbers without anything a lawyer would call consent.

Bilva also had two small but disproportionately loud export relationships. Grace Tan, in Singapore, managed a GCC and South-East Asia distributor network of which Sahil Gulf Trading FZE in Dubai was by far the largest, serving Indian-origin households through Lulu and a long list of independent supermarkets. Vikram Sethi, in New Jersey, ran a North American business selling through Indian grocery chains including Patel Brothers. Between them, exports were ₹13 crore in FY26 — six per cent of revenue, and about a fifth of the gross profit, because GCC pricing carried no trade scheme and no quick-commerce commission.

4. What Happened, and What Was Believed

Through FY25 the Kadam numbers looked like a textbook expansion. Outlets billed rose from 78,000 to 1,42,000; revenue rose 41 per cent to ₹167 crore; the Kaveri covenant tracked comfortably. Internally the belief was simple and unexamined: Bilva had a product that sold well wherever it was placed, so placing it in more shops would produce proportional revenue. Nobody wrote that assumption down, which is why nobody tested it.

The first crack appeared in September 2025 and was misread. Distributor closing stock, which Netra had begun reporting reliably, rose from 28 days to 34. Harish Bhatia attributed it to festive pipeline filling ahead of Diwali, which was a perfectly sound explanation and turned out to be partly true. By March 2026 the number was 41 days and the festive explanation had expired.

The second crack was the panel, restored in January 2026 for Chennai, Hyderabad, Pune and Lucknow. Its first full quarter, reported in April, showed something the company found hard to absorb: in those four cities Bilva's weighted distribution — the share of category sales value represented by stores that stocked Bilva, the ACV measure — had moved only from 41.2 per cent to 44.8 per cent between FY25 and FY26, while numeric distribution in the same cities had risen by more than half. The shops Kadam had added were, in value terms, very small shops. A brand could add 80,000 outlets and buy itself three and a half points of the shelf that mattered.

The third crack was velocity, and it depended entirely on which denominator one used. Measured against outlets billed at least once in the year, general-trade throughput had fallen from ₹663 per outlet per month in FY25 to ₹487 in FY26 — a 27 per cent decline. Measured against outlets billed in the last ninety days, it had fallen from ₹1,207 to ₹1,146, a decline of five per cent. Both numbers were correctly computed from the same ledger. Harish used the second. Priya used the first. Neither had been wrong in any arithmetic sense, and for four months nobody had noticed they were arguing about a denominator.

In July, Katharina Brandt in Berlin, working on pack architecture, asked for the repeat-purchase rate by pack size and was sent a figure of 36 per cent that had appeared in three consecutive board decks. She asked how it was constructed. It took Priya nine days to establish that it was the unweighted average of three digital channels that together accounted for a fifth of revenue, and that for the other four-fifths — every kirana, every DMart shelf — Bilva had never measured repeat purchase at all, and given the absence of any consumer identifier, could not.

In August the modern-trade team received the first of the planogram-reset questionnaires. One national chain asked for rate of sale per facing in the hair-oil bay; Bilva's own audit put it at 6.1 units per store per week against a bay average of 9.4. A second chain asked for share of category value in its stores; Bilva quoted 9.8 per cent from its Netra photographs. The chain's own scan data said 6.4. Nobody at Bilva had been prepared for the possibility that the retailer knew more about the brand's performance than the brand did.

5. The People

Aparna Venkataraman, 38, Head of Product and Category, Chennai, joined in 2023 from a larger personal-care company where she had run a ₹400 crore brand and, crucially, had lived with a full retail panel for six years. She owns both the physical product portfolio and, awkwardly, the Netra roadmap. Her stated position is that the company cannot allocate ₹14 crore sensibly until it agrees on what it is trying to move. What she is not saying: she signed off on the Netra roadmap that de-prioritised a consumer-panel integration twice, in favour of features Harish's team asked for, and she is not certain her present clarity is anything more than hindsight.

Dr. Anil Menon, 57, founder and Managing Director, Coimbatore, is the formulator and the brand's public face. He believes the product's efficacy is self-evident and that any consumer who tries it twice stays. His incentive is the Series C he has been discussing informally since June, which will be priced off FY27 revenue. What he is not saying: he has already told two prospective investors that Bilva will cross three lakh outlets in FY27.

Harish Bhatia, 49, National Sales Head, New Delhi, came from a large FMCG house with a reputation for building distribution fast. He argues that in Indian FMCG, width precedes depth without exception: no brand has ever built velocity in shops it is not in. His variable pay, agreed in 2024, is 60 per cent weighted to outlets billed and secondary sales. What he is not saying: two of the three super stockists he appointed in Uttar Pradesh are carrying stock they have not moved, and he has been quietly extending their credit to keep the billing numbers intact.

Meenakshi Rao, 54, CFO and co-founder, Coimbatore, watches the 41 days of trade stock and the ₹6 crore working-capital limit with the Coimbatore bank. Her position is that the company must not add a rupee of channel inventory this festive season. What she is not saying: the Kaveri covenant is defined on primary dispatch, and a genuine correction of the pipeline would put the company within touching distance of a breach in Q3.

Sneha Kulkarni, 33, Head of Quick Commerce and D2C, Bengaluru, has taken her channel from ₹13 crore to ₹28 crore in a year and has the platform dashboards to prove consumer-level repeat rates nobody else in the company can produce. Her incentive is channel GMV. What she is not saying: after platform commissions, warehousing fees and the ad spend required to hold search position during festive weeks, her channel's contribution margin turned negative in Q4 FY26, and the deck she circulated shows gross margin before those costs.

Priya Ramesh, 31, Data Scientist, Toronto, joined in 2024 and built the velocity and distribution models everyone now argues about. She believes the company should stop spending on reach for two quarters and spend on measurement instead. What she is not saying: her national velocity estimates are extrapolated from four cities using store-universe weights from a 2024 census, and she does not know the size of the error.

Yusuf Shaikh, 41, Engineering Lead, Pune, built Netra and defends it. He has a roadmap item for outlet-level productivity scoring that has slipped three quarters. What he is not saying: the shelf-photograph feature that produces the share-of-shelf number is captured in only 38 per cent of visits, is optional, and the salesmen who capture it earn a visibility incentive.

Grace Tan, 44, Distributor Success Lead, Singapore, has a signed intent from Sahil Gulf Trading in Dubai for ₹18 crore of FY27 offtake in exchange for five-year GCC exclusivity. She argues export velocity per store is eleven times the Indian average. What she is not saying: Sahil Gulf's terms require 90-day credit and four SKUs in GCC-compliant Arabic labelling, and her own bonus is tied to signed distributor commitments rather than to realised sales. Vikram Sethi, 52, in New Jersey, wants the same money spent on North America and has said plainly that he will not accept a GCC exclusivity clause that blocks re-export.

7. Voices

Parachute did not build velocity in shops it was not in. You are showing me a chart that says our new outlets are small. Of course they are small. That is what a new outlet is. Give it eighteen months."

If you use billed outlets we are down twenty-seven. The choice of denominator is the decision. We are pretending it is an input."

Dr. Anil Menon, Coimbatore, 19 September"Aparna, I have great respect for measurement. But I have been in this business thirty years and I have never seen a company grow by counting. We are in two lakh shops. Two years ago we were in seventy thousand. Tell me what number I should be sad about."

8. The Options as Aparna Currently Sees Them

By Sunday evening Aparna had reduced the problem to four options and written each of them on a separate page, which was itself a decision she had not examined.

Option A — buy velocity. Put the ₹9.2 crore of uncommitted money into the 41,000 outlets that already buy ten or twelve months a year: a 45 ml trial pack, a visibility programme paid on audited compliance rather than on photographs, a service-level guarantee so that the third most common reason for a missed sale — the distributor's van did not carry the 200 ml — stops recurring. The argument is that ACV, not outlet count, is what the modern-trade buyer and the consumer actually experience. The weakness is that Bilva has never run a controlled velocity experiment and its 18 per cent lift assumption is, in Priya's phrase, a wish with a decimal point.

Option B — buy width. Take Harish's plan. It is the only option that keeps the Kaveri covenant comfortable, the only one Anil has already promised to investors, and the only one with a history of working in Indian FMCG. It also spends the festive season adding outlets in states where Exhibit 3 suggests the previous cohort has already gone quiet and Illustration 2 suggests velocity is lowest.

Option C — buy the dark stores. Concede that the physical shelf is a slow battle and put the money where the consumer data actually exists. The repeat rates are real, the measurement is clean, the growth is proven. The cost is that the channel does not yet pay for itself, that three platforms can change commercial terms in a quarter, and that a brand with 13 per cent of revenue in quick commerce and 62 per cent in general trade would be starving the larger body to feed the more legible one.

Option D — buy the instrument. Spend ₹3.4 crore on a full national panel subscription and a consumer tracking study, ₹2 crore on a controlled velocity experiment in 4,000 outlets across two states, hold the rest, and go to the board with a plan to decide properly in March. It is the option Priya wants and the only one that admits the company does not know what it is doing. It is also the option that produces no revenue in FY27, and Aparna is aware that she is the executive most likely to be blamed for the measurement gap in the first place.

She had written Grace's GCC proposal as a footnote to all four rather than as an option, on the grounds that ₹6.4 crore of working capital was a different budget. She was not sure that was right either. She was also not sure that four options framed around where to spend ₹14 crore was the right frame at all: the sharpest question in her notebook, written on Friday and not shown to anybody, read what is the one number we would put on the wall — and would we have to change the company to be able to measure it?

9. The Deadline and the Hard Constraints

The board meets at 10 a.m. on Tuesday 22 September in Coimbatore. The Hosur co-packer requires SKU-level line bookings by 3 October for festive production; the 45 ml pack in Option A would additionally need a new mould, a fourteen-week lead time that puts first dispatch in January, after Diwali and after Pongal. Modern-trade planograms freeze in the second week of October and the two national chains have asked for rate-of-sale and category-share submissions by 30 September.

Financially, ₹4.8 crore of the ₹14 crore is contracted against super-stockist minimum guarantees running to March 2027 and cannot be redirected without renegotiating agreements that Harish signed and that carry a termination cost. The working-capital limit with the bank is ₹6 crore and is currently drawn to ₹4.1 crore; ₹21 crore of finished goods sits in the trade. The Kaveri covenant is written on primary dispatch and tested quarterly. A Series C conversation priced on FY27 revenue is live.

On people: there is a hiring freeze below director level until Q3, Priya is the only data scientist and is in Toronto with a nine-and-a-half-hour offset from Coimbatore, and Yusuf's Pune team has committed its next two sprints to the GST e-invoicing changes for the distributor network. On regulation: legal has advised suspending Netra photograph capture pending a DPDP Act consent review, which would remove the company's only continuous source of share-of-shelf data from the end of October; and any efficacy claim used in festive advertising must survive CCPA and ASCI scrutiny, which rules out the growth claim the agency had proposed for the 45 ml pack. Sahil Gulf's exclusivity offer lapses on 31 December.

10. Questions for Discussion

1. Using Exhibits 1, 2 and 3 only, what happened to Bilva's business in FY26? State the answer as a number and name the denominator you chose and why.

2. Exhibits 4 and 5 are each produced by a process with a known bias. For each, describe the bias, say which direction it pushes the number, and say what you would have to do to produce a figure you would sign your name to.

3. Harish argues that width precedes depth and that new outlets are small by definition. What evidence in the case supports him? What evidence would be required to falsify his claim, and does Bilva possess it or could it obtain it before 3 October?

4. Exhibit 6 puts four proposals on a common basis of rupees spent. Is that the right common basis? Construct an alternative comparison and say what it changes about the ranking.

5. Bilva has no consumer identifier in 62 per cent of its revenue and cannot obtain one cheaply. Is repeat purchase therefore the wrong thing for this company to manage, or the right thing badly measured? What would you put in its place, who would own it, on what cadence, and what decision would it inform?

6. It is Monday morning, 21 September. Aparna has one working day and one conversation with Anil Menon before the board. What does she do with it, what does she put in the board note, and what does she say when a director asks her, in front of Harish and Meenakshi, whether the company grew last year?

Eleven Thirty

By half past eleven the lights had come back and the flat was too bright. Aparna put the three printouts in order of how much she trusted them, which took a while, because the one she trusted most was also the one that covered four cities and eight months and had cost the company nothing for twenty months because it had not existed.

She thought about Anil's question and found that she could not answer it honestly in either direction. Two lakh shops was not nothing. Forty-one days of stock was not nothing either. Somewhere between the two was a number that described whether more Indians were putting Bilva oil in their hair this year than last, and the company had spent ₹1.35 crore a year for six years to know that number, and had then spent the same money on an application that could tell her exactly how many photographs a salesman in Patna had uploaded in August.

She opened a blank page for the board note and typed a heading — What we know, what we believe, and what we have been reporting — and then sat looking at it for a long time, aware that all three columns would be different lengths, and that the first one would be the shortest.

Amaltas Foods: Nine Crore Before Diwali

Shruti Nene had ₹9 crore, fourteen days, and three plans on the table. Two of them would raise revenue. Only one of them would keep the brand on the shelf.

1. Baner Road, 12 August 2026

The monsoon had not let up all week, and the eleven o'clock meeting in Amaltas Foods' office off Baner Road in Pune began with the sales team still shaking out umbrellas. Shruti Nene, head of product and category, had called it to settle the festive trade plan. The plan had to be locked by 26 August: Ganesh Chaturthi fell in mid-September, Diwali in the first week of November, and the co-packers in Satara and Indore needed six weeks' notice to reserve line time.

On the table was a budget of ₹9 crore — the largest single allocation Amaltas had ever made — and three competing claims on it. Deepa Krishnan, the national sales head, wanted ₹4.2 crore to appoint two super stockists and add 30,000 general-trade outlets across Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar. Shruti's own team wanted ₹5.1 crore for a 100 g pack, a planogram change and an availability programme in stores Amaltas already served. The quick-commerce team wanted ₹5.6 crore for festive visibility on Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart.

Underneath the three claims sat one email. On 4 August, a category buyer at a large modern-trade chain had asked Amaltas for its rate of sale per facing in the better-for-you snacks bay, ahead of the October planogram reset. The chain's threshold for a permanent listing in that bay was 18 packs per store per week. Amaltas was at 22.4, down from 26.1 the year before. Two more years of the same trend and the number would be a decision made for them.

2. Amaltas Foods

Amaltas was founded in 2018 by Anand Pillai, previously a regional sales manager at a large packaged-foods company, and a food technologist from the Central Food Technological Research Institute in Mysuru. The proposition was simple and, in 2018, unusual: salty snacks made from jowar and ragi rather than potato or corn, baked rather than fried, at price points a kirana could stock. Two products carried the company. Amaltas Jowar Chips, a 70 g pack at ₹40, was the hero SKU and about 60 per cent of revenue. Amaltas Ragi Breakfast Mix, 400 g at ₹210, was the second.

FY26 revenue was ₹96 crore, up from ₹63 crore. Consumer offtake on the hero SKU alone was ₹67.8 crore against ₹43.7 crore the previous year. The company was profitable at the gross level and roughly at break-even after trade and marketing spend.

The competitive field was crowded and well capitalised. In mainstream salty snacks, Haldiram's, Bikaji, Balaji, ITC's Bingo! and PepsiCo's Kurkure and Lay's owned the shelf and the price points. In the better-for-you corner where Amaltas actually competed, Too Yumm, Tata Consumer's Soulfull range and a long tail of regional millet brands fought over a bay that most chains gave between two and four feet. Reliance Retail, Avenue Supermarts' DMart and Spencer's were the modern-trade gatekeepers; Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart had gone from a rounding error to 36 per cent of the hero SKU's offtake in two years. FSSAI's front-of-pack labelling work was a live concern for a brand whose entire claim was nutritional, and GST on the 70 g pack was settled and unremarkable.

3. The situation

In June, Shruti had asked Rahul Menon, Amaltas's data scientist in Toronto, to rebuild the sales model properly. Rahul had spent three years at a retail-measurement firm before joining, and he made one change that altered the conversation: he divided sales not by outlets billed but by outlet-weeks actually in distribution, and he cut the result by channel instead of reporting a national average. The output became Exhibit 1.

The headline was that offtake on the hero SKU had grown 55 per cent, and that every rupee of the growth was explained by new doors. General-trade outlets had gone from 22,800 to 34,600 — a 52 per cent increase — while general-trade rate of sale had fallen from 6.8 to 5.1 packs per outlet-week, a 25 per cent decline. Modern-trade velocity was down from 26.1 to 22.4. Only quick commerce had improved on both counts, and it had done so from a base of 340 dark stores.

Rahul's note, sent at 2 a.m. Pune time on 28 July, put it starkly: "Same-store velocity in general trade is 6.1, not 5.1 — so about half the drop is dilution from the new outlets, which is normal. The other half is real decline in stores we already had. That second half is what I would put in front of Anand."

Two other pieces of evidence had arrived by August. Ishita Raval, Amaltas's designer, working from Berlin and dialling into Pune at 7 a.m. her time, had run a 100 g pack at ₹49 in 220 stores in Nashik through June and July. Portfolio rate of sale in those stores rose from 5.3 to 8.1 packs per outlet-week, and value per outlet-week rose from ₹212 to ₹305. And Kabir Saxena, who ran the international business from New Jersey and supplied a Dubai-based distributor serving the Gulf, had written to say that his buyer wanted the assortment cut to three SKUs, because in his stores the slow movers were being delisted and taking the fast movers' shelf with them.

The last piece was a household panel readout by city, Exhibit 3, which Shruti had commissioned in April and had not yet shown to the sales team.

4. The people

Shruti Nene, 36, head of product and category, Pune. Eight years in packaged foods, two at Amaltas. She owned the trade plan and would present it to the board on 28 August. She wanted the brand to survive the October reset and believed the company had been growing in a way that made that harder.

Deepa Krishnan, 44, national sales head, Mumbai. Twenty years across two large FMCG companies and one failed regional brand. Her team's incentive was on primary billing and outlet additions, and her reputation rested on having built the general-trade network from nothing. She wanted the ₹4.2 crore for the Hindi-belt expansion, and she argued, not unreasonably, that a snack brand that was not in UP was not a national brand.

Rahul Menon, 31, data scientist, Toronto. Wanted the company to adopt rate of sale per outlet-week as its primary operating metric, with a weekly cadence and a named owner. Neutral on which option won, insistent that the decision be made on the same-store number rather than the average.

Ishita Raval, 29, design lead, Berlin. Wanted the ₹49 pack rolled out nationally and the pack's front face redesigned before the FSSAI labelling change forced a laminate changeover anyway. Sceptical of quick-commerce spend, which she described as "renting velocity".

Kabir Saxena, 48, head of international, New Jersey. Wanted SKU rationalisation and a festive gift pack he could sell into the Gulf and the North American ethnic-grocery channel. His business was ₹7 crore and growing, and he pointed out that his margins funded a disproportionate share of the marketing budget.

6. The options

Option A — Hindi-belt expansion (₹4.2 crore). Appoint two super stockists, add 30,000 general-trade outlets across UP, MP and Bihar, fund an introductory scheme and four months of distributor credit. Upside: adds an estimated ₹11 crore of offtake in FY27 and makes the national-brand claim defensible to investors. Cost: at the marginal outlet's likely rate of sale of 2.5 to 3.0 packs a week, it pushes the general-trade average down towards 4.3, raises expiry further, and spends the money in the two markets where Exhibit 3 says the product does not yet repeat.

Option B — Velocity repair in the existing footprint (₹5.1 crore). Roll out the ₹49 100 g pack nationally, negotiate a move from the health-foods aisle to the main snacking bay in 640 modern-trade stores, run sampling in 1,400 high-footfall outlets, and fund an on-shelf-availability programme in the 6,200 general-trade outlets that generate a third of offtake. Upside: if Nashik replicates, portfolio velocity rises roughly 50 per cent, which protects the October listing and lifts every channel at once. Cost: no new outlets, so reported revenue growth in FY27 slows to perhaps 18 per cent, and Deepa's team loses its incentive story for the year.

Option C — Quick-commerce and festive blitz (₹5.6 crore). Buy festive visibility slots, keyword advertising and a ₹299 gift pack across Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart in eleven cities, plus a D2C push. Upside: the fastest and most measurable velocity gain, daily data, and a channel already growing 290 per cent. Cost: platform commission and advertising take contribution margin on incremental volume from 23 per cent to about 4 per cent; the general-trade decline continues unaddressed; and the brand becomes dependent on a channel where assortment is re-decided by an algorithm every week.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, decompose FY26 offtake growth in general trade into a distribution contribution and a velocity contribution. What does the same-store row change about that reading, and what does the returns row change back?

2. Deepa argues that a brand absent from Uttar Pradesh is not a national brand. What would have to be true in Exhibit 3 for that argument to be correct?

3. Exhibit 2 shows three rates of sale against three different thresholds. Which of the three is the binding constraint on Amaltas's next twelve months, and why is the national average of 5.9 packs per outlet-week worse than useless?

4. Shruti must recommend an allocation of ₹9 crore on 26 August. What is her recommendation, what metric will she ask the board to hold her to, and at what cadence and with what named owner?

8. A note for the learner

This case is an exercise in reading three numbers that are routinely collapsed into one. For a physical product, consumer offtake is the product of distribution — how many doors a buyer can find you behind — and velocity, the rate of sale behind each door. Share is a ratio computed afterwards and tells you whether growth was won or granted. The asymmetry that drives the case is that distribution can be bought with money in a quarter, while velocity has to be earned; and the retailer, who controls the distribution, renews you on velocity.

A well-reasoned answer does four things. It closes the identity on Exhibit 1 rather than arguing about the growth rate. It separates the arithmetic dilution of adding weak outlets from genuine decline in existing ones, using the same-store row. It refuses to use a national average velocity when Exhibit 2 shows three channels with different units and different thresholds. And it treats Exhibit 3 as evidence about where expansion will and will not work, rather than as a marketing footnote.

One defensible path. Fund Option B in full at ₹5.1 crore; ring-fence ₹1.5 crore of Option C for festive visibility in the eight cities where Exhibit 3 shows repeat at or above norm, on the argument that quick commerce is the cheapest velocity laboratory Amaltas has; hold ₹1.4 crore for the October planogram negotiation and the FSSAI-driven laminate changeover; and defer Option A to FY28, with one exception — a 3,000-outlet pilot in Lucknow and Kanpur funded from the ₹1.4 crore reserve and explicitly designed as a test of whether the Delhi–Lucknow repeat problem is availability or product. The reasoning is that the binding constraint in the next twelve months is the October threshold, not the absence of UP; that expanding into markets with 14 per cent repeat converts cash into expiry; and that the Nashik result is the only intervention in the case with evidence of lifting velocity rather than borrowing it. Shruti should ask the board to hold her to one number — rate of sale per outlet-week, cut by channel, reviewed every Monday, owned by her rather than by sales — and to accept that FY27 revenue growth will be slower and the brand will still be on the shelf in FY28.

Velocity, Distribution and Share: What Physical Products Actually Report

1. Two rooms, eleven days apart

On 3 November 2026, Devika Menon, vice-president of sales and category at Vrinda Home Care, a ₹880 crore maker of detergent bars and hair-care sachets headquartered in Mumbai, had a term sheet in front of her from a national modern-trade chain. For ₹6.2 crore of annual trade investment — listing fees, a guaranteed secondary display, and two end-caps a quarter — Vrinda's flagship Vrinda Neem Bar would move from partial to full listing across the chain's western footprint. Her commercial finance lead in Pune had modelled it as an increase of about nine points of ACV distribution in the West. Her national sales head, a man who had spent twenty years selling into general trade against Nirma, Ghadi and Hindustan Unilever's Wheel, thought the deal was a trap. Her marketing head thought refusing it was worse than a trap: it was a decision to stay small. Both of them were arguing from the same NielsenIQ file.

Eleven days later and 520 kilometres north-west, on 14 November, Rohit Bhanushali, head of product at Vismay Devices in Ahmedabad, faced a decision with the same metric architecture and completely different economics. Vismay made the Vismay Vahini reverse-osmosis water purifier, sold through roughly 9,200 electronics and general-hardware outlets, and earned most of its money from the Vismay Vishuddh replacement cartridge that a household was supposed to buy about every eight months. Vismay had 4.8 lakh purifiers installed. Rohit's board wanted a ₹1,400 price cut on the purifier to accelerate into tier-three towns, where his distribution was thin and his rate of sale per store was actually higher than in Ahmedabad and Surat. His own data said the towns with the highest purifier velocity had the lowest genuine-cartridge repeat rate, because local workshops refilled cartridges for ₹350. Devika was being asked whether to buy distribution. Rohit was being asked whether the velocity he could buy was worth having. The two questions are the same question, and the discipline that answers it is older than either company.

2. The idea, and the argument inside it

The vocabulary comes from the retail audit. In 1933 A. C. Nielsen began sending auditors into American drugstores to count shelf stock and invoices, and from that physical count he manufactured the concept the industry still runs on: market share measured at the point of sale rather than at the point of shipment. Two structural ideas followed. The first was weighted distribution, usually stated as %ACV — the share of a market's All Commodity Volume, meaning the total retail turnover of every category sold in a store, that occurs in the stores carrying your item. A brand in 20,000 tiny outlets and a brand in 900 supermarkets can have identical %ACV, and that is the point: the measure asks how much shopper traffic you are reachable by, not how many shutters you are behind. The second was rate of sale, also called velocity — units or rupees sold per stocking store per week, computed only across the distributing base, which converts a sales number into a statement about desirability per unit of shelf.

The two combine into the only identity that matters here. A brand's value share equals its weighted distribution multiplied by its share of category sales inside the stores where it is present. Divide share by %ACV and you get sales per point of distribution (SPPD), the diagnostic that every competent category manager computes before speaking. Two further measures sit alongside. Share of shelf is your facings as a percentage of the category's facings, best read as a fair-share index — share of shelf divided by share of sales — because a ratio above 1.0 means the retailer is giving you more space than your sales justify, which is a debt, not a trophy. Repeat rate is the proportion of buyers in one window who buy again in the next, and it is the only one of the four that carries information about the product rather than about the trade.

Three schools disagree about what to do with these numbers, and the disagreement is genuine. The physical-availability school, associated with the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute and Byron Sharp's work, holds that brands grow mainly by being easy to buy for more people; distribution is the dominant causal lever, and velocity largely follows reach because penetration drives everything. It will sign: buy the distribution, the velocity follows. It will not sign: high velocity in a small footprint proves a brand deserves scale. The velocity-first school is the operating belief of modern-trade buyers and of most founders of the last decade: shelf is rationed by rate of sale, so velocity is the currency that purchases distribution, and distribution bought with cash rather than earned with velocity is rented and will be repossessed. It will sign: prove rate of sale in a small base, then expand. It will not sign: distribution causes demand. The third, the incrementality school, refuses both as universal claims and says only a controlled comparison — matched store panels, staggered rollouts, holdout geographies — can establish what a rupee of trade spend actually bought. It will sign: estimate the causal effect or admit you are guessing. It will not sign: observed SPPD predicts marginal SPPD. Devika's meeting contained all three positions and nobody named them.

3. Mechanics: the arithmetic experts run before they argue

Devika's West-region file, covering the twelve weeks to 25 October 2026, is laid out below alongside her nearest branded rival, Wagheri Consumer Brands, whose bar sells at a lower price point and sits in far more outlets.

Table 1 — Vrinda converts each point of distribution into roughly twice the share Wagheri does, and is under-spaced relative to its sales; Wagheri has bought reach and shelf it is not converting.

The naive expansion arithmetic is a single line. Nine incremental points of ACV at the current SPPD of 0.119 implies 1.07 points of value share, which on a ₹2,050 crore category is ₹21.9 crore of incremental value sales. At Vrinda's 22% gross margin that is ₹4.8 crore of gross profit against ₹6.2 crore of trade investment, so the deal loses ₹1.4 crore in year one and the sales head is right. The marketing head's rebuttal is that the deal is an investment whose second year carries no listing fee, and that a bar seen on an end-cap in Mumbai is a bar remembered in a kirana in Nashik.

Both readings are amateur, because both assume the marginal point of distribution behaves like the average point. It never does. Brands are listed in their best-fitting stores first; the stores still unserved are, almost by construction, the ones where the product fits worst. Practitioners handle this with a distribution response curve: plot cumulative share against cumulative %ACV, ordering stores by their velocity for your brand, and the curve is concave. A defensible rule of thumb in Indian home-and-personal-care is that the marginal decile of ACV delivers between 45% and 70% of average SPPD. Apply 60% and the nine points return 0.64 share points, ₹13.2 crore of sales, ₹2.9 crore of gross profit, and the deal is worse than it first looked. Apply the correction in the other direction — modern-trade stores in the West are, for a premium-priced neem bar, better-fitting than Vrinda's average general-trade outlet, plausibly 1.2× average SPPD — and the nine points return 1.29 share points and ₹5.8 crore of gross profit, roughly break-even before any second-year effect.

Two steps are usually left implicit. The first is that %ACV is defined per item, not per brand, so a brand carrying six SKUs has six distribution numbers; the industry aggregates them as total distribution points (TDP), the sum of each SKU's %ACV. TDP rises whenever a SKU is added, which flatters a sales team's dashboard while lowering per-SKU rate of sale, and per-SKU rate of sale is what a retailer's assortment algorithm uses to decide delisting. The second is the distinction between listed and available: an outlet counts as distributing if the auditor finds the item stocked or invoiced, so a store that carries the SKU and is out of stock nine days a month still reports as distribution. On-shelf availability is a separate measurement, and the gap between the two is where most unexplained velocity decay lives.

4. When the framework applies, and when it misleads

The framework rests on three testable conditions. First, shelf must be genuinely scarce and rationed by a third party; if it is, velocity is a currency. Second, the store universe must be measurable and reasonably stable, so that a denominator exists. Third, purchase must be observable at the point of sale rather than only at the point of shipment. Devika satisfies all three cleanly: detergent bars compete for a fixed shelf bay, the universe is audited, and NielsenIQ reads scan and audit data across both channels. Rohit satisfies the first two only partially and the third barely. A water purifier occupies floor space in a mixed-assortment electronics store where the relevant scarcity is the salesman's attention, not the shelf; the universe of such outlets is not audited with anything like grocery precision; and the cartridge, which is the business, is bought in a channel that includes unbranded refillers no panel counts.

The framework becomes actively misleading in three situations. Where the product is bought infrequently and considered heavily — purifiers, mattresses, mixer-grinders — rate of sale per store per week is so low that a store-week is dominated by noise, and managers read random variation as signal. Where the true revenue engine is a consumable or a service annuity, distribution of the durable is a lead-generation metric, not a revenue metric, and optimising it can destroy value if the incremental customers are the least likely to repeat. And where a channel prices and ranks algorithmically — quick commerce, marketplaces — the store universe is one warehouse per catchment, %ACV collapses toward a binary, and the meaningful scarcity migrates to search placement, where the physical vocabulary still works but every number has to be rebuilt.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product portfolios break the arithmetic first. When Vrinda's sachet shampoo and its bar share a distributor and a salesman's call, the incremental ACV bought for one is partly bought for the other, and the trade spend is booked against whichever brand manager negotiated it. Mature companies handle this by measuring distribution at the outlet level across the portfolio and charging trade spend to a channel P&L rather than a brand P&L; most companies say they do this and in practice allocate by revenue weight, which systematically over-rewards the largest brand.

Hardware-plus-consumable businesses such as Vismay invert the hierarchy. The honest metric set is distribution of the purifier, velocity of the purifier, and repeat rate of the cartridge — and the third dominates the first two economically. Rohit's contribution per purifier is ₹2,100; per genuine cartridge it is ₹740, and his installed base buys an average of 2.4 genuine cartridges before the relationship lapses, worth ₹1,776, so nearly half the lifetime value of a customer sits in a metric his sales dashboard does not carry. When the app-connected models report filter life and prompt a reorder, the twelve-month genuine-cartridge rate is 61%; in the non-connected base sold through the same outlets it is 38%. That difference — 23 points of repeat — is worth more than any plausible distribution gain, and it is invisible in the retail-audit view of the business.

Regulated categories add a distribution constraint that is legal rather than commercial: state-level excise for alcohol, licensing for nutraceuticals, and FSSAI labelling changes that can render existing stock unsellable and wipe out weeks of measured velocity. AI-native and software products import the vocabulary loosely — distribution becomes the number of surfaces and integrations a capability is reachable from, velocity becomes usage per active surface, share of shelf becomes prominence in the host application's menu — and the import is useful precisely because software teams under-measure reachability. The seam that hurts everywhere is the same: sales owns distribution, marketing owns share, supply chain owns availability, and nobody owns rate of sale, which is the number that ties them together.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The marginal store is not the average store

The competent manager multiplies SPPD by incremental ACV points. The expert refuses, because SPPD is an average over a non-random sample that the company itself selected for fit. The tell is a distribution plan whose projected share gain is exactly linear in ACV; the expert's first question is which decile of stores the new points come from and what those stores' category throughput looks like. The obvious reading — that a brand converting well should convert well everywhere — is wrong because the conversion was partly caused by the selection.

Distribution is a stock that leaks

Listings churn: outlets close, distributors are changed, a salesman stops calling, a retailer rationalises assortment. In Indian general trade a brand commonly loses two to four points of numeric distribution a quarter without anyone reporting it, because dashboards show gross additions. The tell is a sales team reporting 14,000 new outlets opened while %ACV moves one point. The expert reads net distribution and the age profile of listings; the competent practitioner celebrates the gross number.

The weighted-numeric gap is strategy, not a footnote

Vrinda's 54% weighted against 39% numeric says the brand lives in larger, higher-turnover stores; Wagheri's 71% against 66% says it is spread thin and evenly. The gap tells you which brand is vulnerable to a modern-trade shift and which is vulnerable to a rural push. The tell is a deck that quotes only one of the two; ask which, and why that one.

Unit velocity and value velocity diverge on purpose

A price increase or a pack-size reduction — the grammage cut that Indian FMCG uses instead of raising price points — drops unit rate of sale while value rate of sale holds or rises. The tell is a velocity decline that begins in precisely the week a new pack shipped. The expert indexes rate of sale in rupees per store per week and in grams, and looks at both.

TDP inflation hides per-SKU starvation

Adding variants raises total distribution points and the brand's apparent reach while pushing each SKU's velocity toward the retailer's delisting threshold. The tell is rising TDP with falling average per-SKU rate of sale. The obvious reading, that more variants mean more shelf presence, is wrong: it means more chances to be delisted, and a delisting takes the shelf slot with it.

Phantom distribution is the largest silent loss

Listed and available are different states. A brand at 62% %ACV with 14% out-of-stock in listed outlets is effectively at 53%. The tell is %ACV rising while rate of sale falls by almost exactly the same proportion — a pattern that looks like weakening demand and is usually a replenishment failure. A fifty-store manual audit settles it in a week for under a lakh.

Share of shelf is a liability above a fair-share index of one

Facings are bought as often as earned. A brand holding 1.34 fair share, as Wagheri does, is carrying space the retailer's own category-profit model will eventually reclaim. The tell is a brand whose shelf share has grown faster than its sales share for three consecutive review cycles. The expert treats that as a countdown, not an achievement.

Repeat rate is defined by its window and its base

An eight-week repeat rate and a twelve-month repeat rate differ by twenty points or more on the same product, and a repeat computed only on buyers who appear in the first window structurally excludes late adopters, biasing it downward in a growing brand and upward in a declining one. Panel bases in Indian regional cuts are often under a hundred households. The tell is a repeat figure quoted without a window, a base size and a channel.

Promotional volume is borrowed, not created

A price-off week can double rate of sale and pull forward four weeks of household consumption. Unless velocity is decomposed into baseline and incremental, a brand can run a permanent promotion and believe it has a velocity advantage. The tell is a baseline that steps down after each promotional block. The cost of missing this is a trade-spend ratchet that is politically impossible to reverse.

Distribution and velocity are endogenous to each other

Good products get listed, and listed products get bought, so the correlation between reach and rate of sale proves nothing about direction. This is why the incrementality school exists. The tell is anyone asserting causation from a cross-sectional scatter of stores. The expert's instinct is to withhold entry in a matched set of outlets and compare, which costs a quarter and settles the argument permanently.

7. How the practice changes by product type and company stage

In consumer packaged goods the four metrics are used exactly as described, from audit and panel data. In B2B and enterprise the analogues are real but weaker: distribution becomes active channel partners and covered geographies, velocity becomes bookings per partner per quarter, share of shelf becomes presence in partner proposals and analyst shortlists, and repeat becomes renewal rate — and here the repeat metric dominates so completely that the others are mostly leading indicators. On platforms and marketplaces, distribution is live sellers or listings, velocity is GMV per listing per day, and share of shelf becomes share of search impressions and buy-box wins, which is the one setting where share of shelf is literally auctioned and therefore honestly priced. For hardware and physical durables the numbers apply but the velocity denominator is too thin to be weekly; monthly rate of sale per store and attach rate on the consumable carry the argument. For AI products the mapping is real for reachability and prominence and false for velocity, because usage per surface is not rationed by a third party and there is no shelf to lose.

Stage changes emphasis, not definition. An early brand cannot afford reach and should prove rate of sale and repeat in one city, because those are the two numbers a modern-trade buyer or a distributor will actually underwrite; it treats distribution as a reward. A mid-size company like Vrinda, at 54% ACV, lives in the zone where the distribution response curve is bending and every expansion decision needs the marginal correction. A national incumbent near saturation has no distribution lever left and fights entirely on rate of sale, share of shelf and repeat — which is why the largest Indian FMCG companies spend disproportionately on in-store execution and on-shelf availability rather than on listings.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Example one: the marginal correction, applied. Devika ran the chain deal three ways. At constant SPPD the nine points returned ₹4.8 crore of gross profit; at the conservative 0.6 marginal factor, ₹2.9 crore; at the channel-fit-adjusted 1.2 factor, ₹5.8 crore. None of the three cleared ₹6.2 crore in year one. The decision therefore did not turn on the share arithmetic at all — it turned on whether the second year, which carries roughly ₹2.4 crore of spend rather than ₹6.2 crore, would inherit the distribution. That is a contractual question, not an analytical one.

Example two: the repeat-rate annuity. Rohit modelled the ₹1,400 price cut as a 34% volume lift on purifiers, taking monthly rate of sale from 1.7 to 2.3 units per store. On 9,200 outlets that is about 5,500 extra purifiers a month, but contribution per purifier falls from ₹2,100 to ₹700, so hardware contribution barely moves: 5,500 × ₹700 against the ₹1,400 forgone on the 15,600 units he would have sold anyway, a net loss of about ₹1.8 crore a month before cartridges. The cut is only justified if incremental customers repeat. In his top-repeat districts they buy 2.4 genuine cartridges at ₹740 contribution; in the tier-three towns driving the volume lift, measured repeat is 21%, implying about 0.9 cartridges and ₹666. The price cut therefore buys the customers least able to fund it.

Example three: the failure, and the recovery. Vyapti Foods, a ₹210 crore breakfast-cereal company, spent eighteen months driving national %ACV from 31 to 68 on a sell-in-based incentive scheme, and reported record shipments throughout. Two things were true underneath. Its SKU count had gone from 11 to 34, so TDP looked spectacular while average per-SKU rate of sale fell from 5.9 to 2.1 units per store per week. And an on-shelf-availability audit in January 2026 found 41% of listed outlets out of stock on the lead SKU, because distributor stock had been pushed to hit slabs and had aged. Returns and expiry write-offs reached ₹19 crore in a single half-year, roughly 9% of revenue. The recovery took three quarters: Vyapti cut back to 11 SKUs, deliberately delisted about 12,000 low-throughput outlets, moved the incentive scheme from primary to secondary sales, and accepted %ACV falling to 44. Per-SKU rate of sale rose to 6.8, write-offs fell to under ₹3 crore, and value share — the number nobody had been managing — ended 40 basis points higher than at peak distribution.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings and the cost of a late catch

Sell-in masquerading as sell-through is the costliest. The early warning is distributor days-of-inventory rising while audited rate of sale is flat; the diagnostic question is simply whether the growth number on the slide is primary or secondary sales; caught at quarter two it costs a missed target, caught at quarter six it costs Vyapti's ₹19 crore. Phantom distribution announces itself as %ACV and rate of sale moving in opposite directions by similar proportions; the diagnostic is a fifty-store availability audit. SKU proliferation shows up as rising TDP with falling per-SKU velocity; the question to ask is what each SKU's rate of sale is against the chain's delisting threshold, and catching it late means losing the bay, not just the variant. Buying shelf in low-ACV outlets shows up as a fair-share index above one in stores contributing under 0.2% of category ACV each; rank outlets by ACV contribution before allocating a rupee. And a thin-panel repeat rate shows up as a suspiciously round, suspiciously high number; ask for the base, the window and the channel, and if the base is under a hundred households, commission a refresh before committing seven figures against it.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is causal. The physical-availability position, in its strongest form, rests on decades of panel evidence that brands of similar share have similar loyalty and that share differences are overwhelmingly penetration differences; on that evidence, distribution is not a reward for velocity but the mechanism by which velocity is produced, and a brand that waits to earn shelf will be out-grown by one that buys it. It would be wrong if marginal distribution routinely delivered SPPD far below average and if bought listings decayed quickly — both of which are observable, and both of which happen in Indian general trade. The velocity-first position rests on the fact that retailers delist on rate of sale and that rented distribution shows measurable decay; it would be wrong if the cost of reach were falling fast enough that decay no longer mattered, which is arguably true in quick commerce, where listing is cheap and reversible.

The second disagreement is about measurement itself. One camp holds that retail-audit panels remain the only comparable, cross-brand truth, because first-party data covers only your own sales and tells you nothing about share. The other holds that with e-commerce and quick commerce now a material and fast-growing share of urban Indian packaged-goods sales, and with general-trade estimates projected from samples, the audit universe is drifting from reality faster than it is being re-based, so brands should run on first-party and platform data and treat audited share as a lagging sanity check. The evidence for the second position is that audited and platform numbers now diverge routinely in metros; the evidence for the first is that no brand has yet demonstrated a reliable way to estimate category share without a panel. Nobody in the field holds a synthesis of these two views; they hold one and tolerate the other.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this quotes %ACV and rate of sale correctly. Someone who has internalised it never quotes a distribution number without its numeric twin, never quotes a velocity number without saying which stores are in the denominator and whether it is units or rupees, and never quotes a repeat rate without a window and a base. They ask where the marginal point of distribution is coming from before they ask what it costs. They treat an over-index on shelf share as a debt. They know which of their numbers is the noisy one and they show the decision flipping when it moves, rather than defending the point estimate. And they hold the causal question open: they design a matched-store holdout when the stakes justify a quarter of patience, because they know that every clean-looking cross-section in this field is contaminated by the company's own past decisions.

12. What each protagonist decided

Devika signed a modified deal. Because none of her three scenarios cleared the first-year spend, she refused to treat the arithmetic as the argument and negotiated the thing the arithmetic depended on: a two-year term with listing fees front-loaded into year one and a contractual assortment guarantee for year two, plus a clause tying the second end-cap to a rate-of-sale threshold she believed she could clear. She also carved ₹35 lakh out of the trade budget for a matched-store holdout in forty outlets across two districts, so that next year's version of this argument would have a causal estimate in it rather than three assumptions. Rohit declined the price cut and proposed instead that the same margin be spent making every Vismay Vahini connected, because 23 points of cartridge repeat was worth more than any distribution he could buy, and because the towns his board was excited about were the towns where the annuity leaked fastest.

Three questions worth arguing before the next case. First: if distribution and velocity cause each other, on what evidence should a company ever act — and what is the fair price of the quarter it costs to find out? Second: when shelf share and listings can simply be purchased, what should the word "performance" mean in a physical channel, and which of the four metrics is hardest to buy? Third: Rohit's most valuable metric is not measured by anyone outside his company, and Devika's most valuable metric is measured by an outside panel she does not control — which of them is in the more dangerous position?

13. Going deeper

North Star metric is the parent question: velocity and distribution are the physical-goods inputs a consumer company assembles into a single directional number, and seeing how they roll up prevents treating them as ends. Reading retail scan and sell-through data is the immediate practical next step — it teaches the file formats, the projection methods and the channel definitions that sit under every number above, and it is where the sell-in versus sell-through distinction becomes concrete. Category management takes the argument up a level: it is how assortment, shelf and promotion are decided across a whole category, and it explains why a retailer might rationally delist a brand with good velocity. What makes a good metric and vanity versus actionable metrics together explain why TDP and gross outlet additions survive in dashboards despite being poor decision inputs. The GAME framework and acquisition, retention and monetisation actions give the structure for tying each metric to an owner, a cadence and a decision — the discipline that would have caught Vyapti's problem a year earlier. Direct versus proxy, magnitude versus ratio is the sharpest lens on SPPD and the fair-share index, both of which are ratios whose numerator and denominator move for independent reasons. And attention, transaction and productivity games explains why the physical vocabulary transfers cleanly to some digital products and misleads badly in others.

CPG Metrics: Velocity, Distribution, and Share

A budget, two states, and one number missing from the deck

On the last Monday of September 2026, Ananya Rao sat in a glass-walled meeting room in Godhuli Foods' Bengaluru office with a decision she had eleven days to make. Godhuli, a fourteen-year-old maker of namkeen and packaged snacks with roughly ₹340 crore in annual revenue, had been given an incremental ₹40 lakh in trade marketing budget by the CFO to spend before Diwali, and Ananya, as the company's head of category management, had to decide whether that money went to Karnataka, where Godhuli's flagship Sev Mix already sat in a large number of stores, or to Tamil Nadu, where the brand was in far fewer stores but seemed to be selling unusually well wherever it was. Her regional sales heads had opposite instincts. The Karnataka head wanted the money to fight for better shelf position against Haldiram's and a fast-growing rival called Kadak Snacks. The Tamil Nadu head wanted it to fund new store openings, arguing that the brand was "flying off the shelf" wherever it existed. Both were using the word "performance" to mean different things, and Ananya realised the deck in front of her had sales totals by state but nothing that separated how many stores stocked the product from how fast it moved once it was there. Without that separation, she could not tell whether Tamil Nadu's smaller sales number reflected a weak product or simply a market Godhuli had not yet bothered to enter properly, and a wrong guess would not just waste ₹40 lakh; it would cost Godhuli a full quarter of the pre-Diwali selling season it could not repeat.

The idea: three questions physical goods must answer separately

Velocity, distribution, and share are three of the handful of metrics that retail-audit firms such as Nielsen (now NielsenIQ) built in the mid-twentieth century to answer a problem digital products do not have: a physical product cannot be bought unless it is physically present somewhere a shopper can reach it, and being present is not the same as being wanted. Distribution, most precisely measured as ACV (All Commodity Volume) distribution, is the percentage of a market's total retail sales value that occurs in stores which stock your product — a weighted measure of reach, not a raw store count. Rate of sale (also called velocity) is how fast a product sells once it is on the shelf, typically expressed as units sold per store per week. Share of shelf is the fraction of physical shelf space or facings your product occupies relative to competitors in the same set. And repeat rate is the percentage of first-time buyers who purchase the product again within a defined window, the closest physical-goods proxy to retention. The sentence Ananya could say in a meeting without sounding glib is this: distribution gets you into the store; velocity decides whether you stay.

How the four metrics are actually built

Practitioners rarely spell out the arithmetic behind these numbers, which is exactly where newcomers go wrong. ACV distribution is not "how many shops carry this SKU" divided by "how many shops exist." It is the combined retail turnover of the stores that carry the SKU, divided by the combined retail turnover of every store in the relevant universe — so a product sitting in five hundred large supermarkets can have higher ACV distribution than a product sitting in five thousand tiny kirana stores, because the denominator is weighted by each store's overall size, not counted store by store. Rate of sale is then computed only across the stores where the product is actually stocked: total units sold in a period, divided by the number of distributing stores, divided by the number of weeks in that period. Share of shelf comes from physical audits — a merchandiser or a retail-audit panel counts facings (the number of shelf slots a SKU occupies) in a sample of stores and expresses your count as a percentage of all facings in that category set. Repeat rate is pulled from consumer panel data (household panels of the kind Kantar Worldpanel runs) or, increasingly, from loyalty-card and quick-commerce app data, tracking the same households or accounts across two purchase windows. The step people leave implicit is that each of these four numbers is measured over a different population — the store universe, the distributing subset, the audited sample, and the buyer panel — and comparing them without noting that is where most of the errors below begin.

Running the numbers for Godhuli Sev Mix

Ananya pulled NielsenIQ retail-audit data for September 2026 covering the packaged namkeen category in both states. In Karnataka, the category's total addressable outlet universe carried a combined ACV of ₹1,240 crore; Sev Mix was listed in outlets whose combined ACV came to ₹520 crore, giving an ACV distribution of 520/1,240 = 41.9%. Raw numeric distribution, by contrast, was only 37.5% (34,500 of 92,000 outlets) — a five-point gap showing the brand skewed toward larger, higher-turnover stores, a distinction worth noting on its own. Over the four weeks of September, those 34,500 stores sold 3,10,000 units combined, giving a rate of sale of 3,10,000 ÷ 34,500 ÷ 4 = 2.25 units per store per week. In Tamil Nadu, distribution was much thinner: an ACV distribution of only 26%, in stores that between them sold enough volume to produce a rate of sale of 3.4 units per store per week — roughly 50% faster velocity, in far fewer stores.

To decide where ₹40 lakh does more good, Ananya built a rough opportunity score: the untapped share of the market (1 minus ACV distribution) multiplied by rate of sale multiplied by repeat rate, as a proxy for how much incremental, sticky volume a rupee of distribution spend could unlock. For Karnataka: (1 − 0.419) × 2.25 × 0.34 = 0.444. For Tamil Nadu: (1 − 0.26) × 3.4 × 0.51 = 1.283 — nearly three times higher, because Tamil Nadu combined the largest reachable gap with the fastest sell-through and the strongest evidence that buyers, once they tried Sev Mix, kept buying it. But Ananya then ran a second pass, changing only the repeat-rate input, because it was based on a thin household-panel sample. If Tamil Nadu's true repeat rate were 20% rather than 51%, the score fell to 0.74 × 3.4 × 0.20 = 0.503 — still ahead of Karnataka, but barely. If repeat fell further, to 12%, the score dropped to 0.302, below Karnataka's 0.444, flipping the recommendation entirely. One shaky input, repeat rate, was doing more work in the decision than either distribution or velocity.

Seven distinctions a learner has to sit with

ACV distribution is not the same as numeric distribution

A brand can be in thousands of small stores and still show low ACV distribution, or in relatively few large stores and show high ACV distribution, because ACV weights by each store's total commodity turnover, not by how many stores exist. Sales teams love to quote whichever number looks better, and a newcomer should always ask which one is on the slide.

Rate of sale must be measured only where the product is actually stocked

Dividing total units sold by the entire store universe, rather than by the distributing subset, silently understates velocity in a market where distribution is thin, making a genuinely fast-selling product look sluggish simply because it was compared against stores that never had a chance to sell it.

Sell-in is not sell-through

What a distributor orders from the factory (sell-in) and what a shopper actually buys off the shelf (sell-through, the basis of true rate of sale) can diverge for months, especially near a trade scheme deadline, and a company that tracks only sell-in can be shipping inventory into a market that is quietly not selling it.

Share of shelf is negotiated, not only earned

Facings are frequently bought through trade spend and retailer relationships rather than purely won through consumer pull, so a rising share of shelf can reflect a bigger cheque this quarter rather than a stronger brand, and it should be read alongside rate of sale, not instead of it.

Repeat rate is extremely sensitive to the window and the base

An 8-week repeat rate and a 52-week repeat rate on the same product can differ by twenty points or more, and a repeat rate calculated on forty households in a thin panel carries a margin of error wide enough to reverse a decision, as Ananya's second pass showed.

Retail-audit data has real sampling noise, especially in general trade

Modern-trade chains report near-exact point-of-sale data, but the fragmented kirana channel is usually estimated from a sample of audited stores projected across the universe, so a single-digit swing in a general-trade-heavy state can be noise rather than signal.

None of these four numbers explains profitability or motive

A product can show excellent velocity purely because it is being discounted below a sustainable margin, or excellent distribution purely because a distributor is over-ordering to hit a slab incentive; velocity, distribution, and share describe movement, not whether that movement is healthy.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace, and company stage

In consumer packaged goods the four metrics look exactly as described above, built from retail audits and household panels. In B2B, the same logic reappears in different clothing: "distribution" becomes the number of active reseller or channel-partner relationships and the geographies they cover; "velocity" becomes revenue booked per partner per quarter; "share of shelf" becomes a company's presence and prominence inside partners' proposals and RFP shortlists; and "repeat rate" becomes contract renewal or reorder rate. In a marketplace such as a quick-commerce app or an online retailer, distribution is the number of live sellers or SKUs carrying the category, velocity is GMV per listing per day, share is visibility in search and checkout, and repeat is buyer repurchase rate on the platform. Company stage changes the emphasis more than the metrics themselves: an early-stage brand cannot afford broad distribution and typically proves velocity and repeat rate in one city or one state before spending on reach, essentially treating distribution as the reward for already-proven pull; a large incumbent like ITC or Britannia already sits near saturation on ACV distribution nationally, so its entire battle for growth shifts to rate of sale and share of shelf within stores it is already in.

Where this goes wrong

The first common mistake is chasing a headline ACV percentage while ignoring on-shelf availability — a brand can show 70% ACV distribution and flat sales because a large share of those "distributing" stores are frequently out of stock; the cheapest diagnostic is a spot on-shelf-availability audit of fifty stores rather than trusting the listing number. The second is comparing rate of sale across regions or time periods without adjusting for pack size or price changes, which makes a unit-based velocity number crash after a price increase even though value sales are healthy; recomputing rate of sale in rupees rather than units usually catches this immediately. The third is celebrating a strong repeat rate calculated on a tiny panel base without checking the sample size, which Ananya's own experience showed can overturn a decision once corrected. The fourth is fighting hard for shelf share in stores that contribute little to category ACV, which wins a visible battle while ignoring the handful of large-format stores that actually move the volume; ranking stores by their ACV contribution before allocating trade spend is the standard fix.

What good looks like

A category manager doing this well at a company like Godhuli would not present state-level sales totals at all. She would open with ACV distribution and numeric distribution side by side, follow with rate of sale computed strictly over the distributing base, show share of shelf from a recent audit next to named competitors, and pair repeat rate with its panel size so nobody mistakes a small sample for certainty. She would flag which inputs are noisy and show, as Ananya did, how the recommendation moves if that noisy input turns out to be wrong. The decision that follows is not dramatically different from an ordinary sales review, but it is defensible in a way a single sales number never is, because everyone in the room can see exactly which lever is being pulled and why.

What Ananya decided

Ananya recommended Tamil Nadu for the bulk of the ₹40 lakh, but not on the strength of the headline opportunity score alone. Because the recommendation flipped once repeat rate dropped below roughly 15%, she first spent a modest ₹3 lakh commissioning a quick consumer-panel refresh in the state to confirm the 51% figure before committing the rest, and structured the remaining spend to expand ACV distribution into the next tier of Tamil Nadu outlets in phases, checking rate of sale after each phase rather than releasing the full budget at once. Karnataka's shelf-share fight against Haldiram's and Kadak Snacks was deferred to the following quarter, reframed as a separate decision requiring its own evidence rather than an emotional response to a competitor's shelf position. The next thing worth learning, for anyone following this reasoning further, is category management — how a company decides which SKUs deserve shelf space at all, and how that decision interacts with the four metrics above. Two questions worth sitting with: if a brand's rate of sale is excellent but its repeat rate is unknown, how much should that velocity actually be trusted? And when distribution and shelf share are things a company can simply buy from a retailer, what should "earned" performance in a physical channel actually mean?
